A character may be born into a farming family and become a merchant, warrior, or counsellor to a sovereign, while an heir destined for a distinguished office may lose his possessions and be forced to learn an ordinary trade to survive. Historical circumstances play a considerable role in such changes, particularly when war destroys settlements, migration leads a community into unknown lands, or a new power transforms the institutions of a kingdom. Men nevertheless possess the ability to respond to these events through personal choices, sometimes continuing the traditions they have received, sometimes seeking a path their loved ones had never imagined.

The virtues and shortcomings of the Hildor are as diverse as their ways of life. Courage may arise from the wish to protect a family, ambition from the desire to improve one's circumstances, and prudence from experience acquired through difficult years. The same circumstances may also foster mistrust, pride, or brutality, particularly when individuals have grown up in communities where violence and rivalry hold an important place. A traditional upbringing may form a character devoted to duty, but also one incapable of understanding foreign customs. Travel, encounters, and ordeals allow these convictions to be tested against new situations, giving human characters the opportunity to develop rapidly over the course of their adventures.

The brevity of their existence lends particular significance to these transformations. A Man must often make decisions with the knowledge and resources available to him, without being able to wait several decades to measure all their consequences. He may nevertheless accomplish remarkable works, form lasting friendships, and pass on to his descendants knowledge or obligations whose influence will endure long after his death. This relationship with time explains some of the energy with which the Hildor undertake journeys, establish settlements, and defend their aspirations. It does not, however, impose any particular destiny upon them: some wish to leave behind a great achievement, while others seek only a peaceful existence devoted to those they love and the occupations they have chosen.

Playing a Human

Playing a Human in Middle-earth means portraying a character whose identity is shaped by origins, education, and the experiences that have marked his life. The diversity of the Hildor offers an especially wide range of possibilities, for their Race encompasses peoples whose societies, resources, and traditions may differ profoundly. A character may belong to a woodland community, a farming village, a merchant city, a horse-riding people, or a population established in regions far removed from the lands familiar to the western tales. Birthplace influences knowledge, habits, and relationships with other peoples, while family history often determines the first responsibilities to be faced. These elements provide the starting point for portraying the character, but the events that lead him to embark upon an adventure gradually allow him to discover new possibilities.

A young Woodman may have grown up in a community of Rhovanion, where he learned to recognise forest paths, the animals pursued by hunters, and the places where inhabitants gather the resources needed for survival. He knows the seasons, the dangers of the surrounding lands, and the precautions necessary for travel, but may have little experience of cities and foreign peoples. His departure may be prompted by a poor harvest, the disappearance of a relative, or the desire to find work with a caravan. He may also wish to discover communities established beyond the forests, which he knows only through the stories brought by merchants. His knowledge will prove valuable when crossing wilderness, but the customs of a city or the obligations of a commercial contract may seem far more difficult to understand.

A young woman of Dorwinion may have grown up in a merchant family, surrounded by goods, contracts, and relationships maintained with customers in several regions. She has learned arithmetic, how to assess the quality of certain products, and the conditions necessary for a successful exchange. Her ambition may be to establish commercial connections of her own, reach a distant city, or discover markets to which her family has never sent merchandise. Her knowledge allows her to converse with travellers and understand the practices of commerce, but she must still learn the dangers of the roads, the difficulties of navigation, and the precautions required when negotiating within a community whose traditions are unfamiliar to her. Her adventure may arise from a particularly important contract, the search for a missing business partner, or the desire to establish an enterprise independent of her parents' affairs.

A horseman of Rohan may have been raised in the traditions of caring for horses and serving his lord. He knows the grazing grounds, the roads of his territory, and his family's obligations, but his personal experience depends upon the activities in which he has participated. He may have received military training, accompanied patrols, or devoted most of his time to breeding and watching over herds. His departure may result from an oath, a mission entrusted to him by his lord, or a quarrel with a member of his community. He may seek a missing mount, accompany travellers, or search for a relative who departed several years earlier. His relationships with his people may profoundly influence his decisions, particularly when a family obligation conflicts with commitments made to his companions.

An inhabitant of Harad may possess a very different experience. He may have grown up in a trading city, among the farmers of a fertile region, or within a community that regularly travels across extensive territories. He knows the customs of his people, the routes frequented by merchants, and the conditions necessary for travel in his surroundings. A character from a southern port may have learned several languages and be more familiar with ships, merchandise, and negotiations than with battlefields. His adventure may begin when he embarks upon a distant voyage, seeks to establish new trade relations, or leaves a region troubled by war. The peoples he encounters may regard his clothing, beliefs, or language with curiosity or even mistrust, while he himself discovers traditions previously unknown to him.

A young Man belonging to a people of Rhûn may have grown up in a society whose customs are almost entirely unknown to the peoples of the West. He knows his obligations towards his relatives, the relationships between neighbouring communities, and the traditions to which his family remains attached. His journey may arise from a commercial mission, a migration, a conflict with the authorities of his homeland, or the search for a missing person. The strangers he meets may know nothing of his language or customs, while he discovers peoples whose names were scarcely familiar to him. Such differences may cause misunderstandings, but also allow him to form new relationships and recognise admirable qualities in individuals whom his upbringing had taught him to mistrust.

A character from the Lossoth may possess extensive knowledge of the cold regions of Forochel. He knows how to recognise dangerous weather conditions, prepare for travel across snow, and find the resources necessary to survive in a harsh environment. These skills grant him a considerable advantage in his homeland, but he may be bewildered by the customs of a great southern city, the density of its population, or the demands of trades whose practices he has never witnessed. His departure may be connected with a mission entrusted to him by his community, the search for particular goods, or the desire to discover lands beyond the regions he knows. The encounters he experiences will allow him to acquire new knowledge, without diminishing the importance of his experience of snow and the broad northern wilderness.

Other characters grow up in less fortunate circumstances. A child may have lost his parents during a war and been taken in by another family, while a young Man from a displaced community seeks a territory where his people can settle permanently. A descendant of a ruined family may wish to recover prosperity through commerce, military service, or the practice of a trade, while a character raised under a sovereign hostile to the Free Peoples may have grown up knowing no other political order. Childhood circumstances shape habits and convictions, but do not necessarily determine the future. A character may seek to preserve his family's traditions, make amends for a wrong committed by his relatives, or build a life different from the one events seemed to have prepared for him.

The personal motivations of the Hildor are as diverse as their origins. Some wish to protect loved ones, honour an oath, or fulfil a task entrusted to them by their community, while others seek wealth, recognition, power, or the chance to escape a life they consider too confining. A character may leave home to learn a trade, seek a master, or pursue studies impossible to undertake in his village. Another may wish to find a missing relative, discover his family's origins, or return to a region abandoned by his ancestors. Family obligations frequently provide important reasons for adventure, particularly when a character has left behind people who depend upon his assistance. He may need to send home part of his earnings regularly, find a solution to a debt incurred by his relatives, or fulfil a promise made before his departure.

A character's relationship with authority also offers many opportunities for roleplaying. Someone raised to respect chiefs may find it difficult to disobey a superior, even when the instructions seem unjust, while another, having experienced the violence of arbitrary power, seeks above all to preserve his independence. Discovering other societies may change these convictions. A Man accustomed to decisions made by a hereditary sovereign may be surprised by a community where elders deliberate collectively, while a merchant raised in a city discovers the personal obligations binding members of a clan. Such encounters allow characters to compare inherited teachings with the conduct they observe and gradually develop their own understanding of relations between peoples.

The brevity of human existence lends particular importance to the years spent adventuring. A prolonged journey may represent a considerable part of a character's youth, and the companions he meets, the wounds he suffers, or the decisions he makes may permanently transform his future. He may return to his homeland and discover that his parents have aged, his friends have established families, or the responsibilities he might have received have been entrusted to others. He may also find a new community, acquire knowledge he will later pass on, or form friendships whose value far exceeds the wealth he hoped to obtain when leaving home. Where an Elf may pursue an undertaking across several human generations, a Man must often decide with the knowledge and means available to him in the present, giving his choices a particularly immediate significance.

The Professions available to the Hildor reflect the diversity of their occupations and traditions. A Fighter may belong to the forces of a kingdom, a company of mercenaries, or the defenders of a village, while a Ranger may have learned to cross wilderness, recognise tracks, and protect travellers. A Rogue may possess considerable experience of travel, negotiation, and situations requiring caution, while a Thief may have acquired his skills in city districts, marketplaces, or through a life marked by material hardship. A Bard may preserve the tales of his people, learn languages, and travel to gather the traditions of distant communities. Other Professions are available according to the compatibilities established by MERP-UI, and magical arts may be studied when a Culture, an appropriate education, and a Profession permit access to them. The Human Race does not naturally direct its members towards any of these paths: their particular abilities arise from training, developed talents, and the customs of their communities.

The choice of Age is also decisive in the character's history. During the First Age, he may belong to the earliest human communities, take part in the migrations westward, or live among the Edain allied with the Elves of Beleriand. During the Second Age, he may belong to peoples who remained in Middle-earth, participate in exchanges with Númenórean settlements, or live in a territory subjected to Sauron's influence. During the Third Age, he may belong to the many human Cultures occupying the regions of the North, West, South, or East, while the Fourth Age offers opportunities to participate in the reconstruction of kingdoms, the establishment of new communities, or the exploration of territories long made dangerous by war. Each period determines the peoples he may encounter, the events preserved in his family's memory, and the possibilities open to him.

The Humans — Hildor Race is available in MERP-UI throughout the four Ages of Middle-earth. It represents the shared nature of humanity, including its mortal constitution, general characteristics, and capacity to develop a wide variety of skills. The choice of a Culture then determines the character's origins, education, traditions, languages, and abilities acquired within his community. The Dúnedain, whose Númenórean heritage grants them particular characteristics, are represented separately in MERP-UI. This distinction preserves the diversity of human peoples while maintaining a common racial foundation, in accordance with the principles of the RMU system.

Before approving character creation, the player and Gamemaster should determine the character's people of origin, community, family, the trades he has learned, and the obligations to which he remains bound. They should also establish the events that led him to leave home, the relationships he maintains with his companions, and the aspirations that will guide his decisions. Membership of a Culture provides a historical and social framework, but personality must arise from experience and choice. He may wish to protect his family, discover the world, acquire knowledge, serve a cause, establish a home, attain a new position, or leave behind a work from which others may benefit. The events of his adventure will allow him to weigh these aspirations against inherited responsibilities and decide what he wishes to accomplish during the years granted to him.

The Hildor share a mortal existence and the freedom to choose how they will use the time allotted to them. Their peoples have raised kingdoms, endured wars, and transformed the lands in which they settled, while successive generations have passed down the knowledge and traditions necessary for their survival. Every Man receives part of this inheritance and contributes in turn to the history of Middle-earth. The bonds he preserves, the responsibilities he accepts, and the deeds he performs will determine what he leaves to those who come after him.
